speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: asked the Minister for Trade and Industry (a) what percentage of electricity in Singapore today is from renewables; and (b) how does the investments by local utility companies in overseas renewable projects help Singapore to offset our carbon footprint.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: However, electricity demand will rebound as the economy recovers and grows.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is also driven by new users, such as data centres, 5G telecommunication networks, agri-tech facilities as well as electric vehicles.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will harness the four switches to transform and diversify our energy supply.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is to help us achieve our vision of a clean and efficient energy future.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These four switches comprise natural gas, solar energy, regional power grids and emerging low-carbon alternatives like hydrogen.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Singapore has progressively transitioned from oil-powered power plants since the early 2000s to adopt natural gas.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We do not have the natural resources, land area as well as climatic conditions necessary for the large-scale deployment of renewable energy sources, such as hydro and wind.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Natural gas will continue to be the mainstay and main source of energy for power generation to serve our households and industry reliably in the medium term, and this is as we continue to develop the other three switches.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our second switch, which is solar energy, is currently the most viable source of renewable energy within Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, by 2030, we expect our second switch to supply around 3% of our total electricity consumption.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And, of course, depending on the state of technology at that point in time and cost, we hope to be able to do more.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our local companies partner the Government in the deployment of solar photovoltaic systems.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For example, the Sunseap Group is a major participant in the SolarNova programme, which deploys solar panels in public sector buildings and spaces.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: When these companies invest in overseas renewable companies and projects, they can bring valuable insights and capabilities back home here in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These projects may, some day, also export electricity to Singapore as well.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This brings me, therefore, to the third switch, and that is on regional power grids.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Regional power grids, or electricity imports, is our third switch.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Today, some Southeast Asian countries have an abundance of hydroelectric power and other renewable energies.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If we can connect the regional grid well, it will provide greater resilience and sustainability for the entire system.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: One hundred megawatts would be about 1.5% of our peak electricity demand.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, there will be minimal impact on the reliability as well as cost of our electricity supply.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our preference, of course, is to import electricity from renewable energy sources.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Hence, the “cleanliness” of the generation source will be a consideration in selecting the importer.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Energy Market Authority (EMA) will select the importer through an open and competitive selection process, and it is expected to sell electricity via the Singapore Wholesale Electricity Market (SWEM) to interested buyers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Other companies, like Sun Cable, have also approached EMA to import electricity to Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We welcome these interests, but we have to also be mindful to pace these imports to ensure that they complement and do not undermine the reliability of our electricity supply as well as the stability of our electricity market.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: At this particular point in time, EMA is unable to share details, given the commercial sensitivities – a point that I believe everyone in the House would appreciate.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Last but not least, for our fourth switch, we are also working intensively with the industry and research community to study emerging low-carbon technologies, such as hydrogen and carbon capture, utilisation and storage.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: By tapping on all four switches, Singapore will be able to diversify our energy sources.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This will enhance our access to secure and competitively priced energy supplies and this will reduce our energy security risks.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The future energy mix will depend on technological advances in the four switches.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This will need to be complemented by efforts to enhance energy efficiency across all sectors and consumers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Government will work hand-in-hand with our workforce, researchers, industries and consumers, to achieve our vision of a cleaner, a more efficient and a more secure energy future.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The first question is in relation to energy resilience, and I would like to point out that the Minister had shared and answered some of the questions that I had in mind for my supplementary question.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But the question I have now is, the Minister mentioned that the energy mix would be dependent on the technology improvements over time, but can you roughly share the percentages target for some of these switches at this point in time.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Because if you look at the electricity reliance now, we are relying a lot on natural gas.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think more than 95% of the electricity generated in Singapore is via imported natural gas and it is largely from Malaysia and Indonesia.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, there is a concentration effect, by country, on Malaysia and Indonesia.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The mix by country, for one, if you can share, going forward over the medium to long term, and also in terms of the switches, if you can share.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My second question is, as we proceed to these four switches, going forward – over the next five, 10, 20, 30 and 50 years – for example, in Malaysia's case where we are trying to get the electricity imports from Malaysia into 2021, we have the electricity connector infrastructure with Malaysia.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Going forward if the Sun Cable project does materialise, how do we get some of this direct electricity connectivity to Singapore, when we have these switches exposing us to various countries as far afield as Australia, if the Sun Cable project does happen and as far afield as Indochina, going forward?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, from 65 million tonnes, we will halve it to 33 million tonnes by 2050.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: By the latter half of this century, we will achieve a net zero carbon emission.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: That is the target that we have set for ourselves.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Depending on the technology development over the next 10,15 to 20 years, we should see an increased migration towards renewable energy, of which solar is one of them, and a higher degree, depending on the trial import of this 100 megawatt from Peninsular Malaysia, a higher reliance on drawing from the regional power grid as well.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In fact, just last year, declared our intent to procure another 100 megawatt from the Lao PDR via the Lao, Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore grid network.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We hope that in time, we can also, through this, reach out to more ASEAN countries to tap on this regional grid.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: That is another one of our diversification strategies.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To the extent that we are able to draw from the regional power grid, we certainly would.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Sun Cable project, as I have alluded to, is also something which we are in active negotiations.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Obviously, we are not at liberty at this particular point in time to communicate the details of it because of the commercial sensitivities.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To the Member's last point about the concentration risk, today, a significant amount of the natural gas that we are using to burn comes from Malaysia and Indonesia through the PNG.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But we have also now diversified the sources of the procurement via LNG, the liquefied natural gas, from other countries further afield and that includes the Middle East, UAE and so on.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The exact breakdown of that, at this particular point in time, I cannot provide to the hon Member.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The first is in relation to the setting off targets.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I note the Minister's speech that we are expected to employ two gigawatt peaks of solar energy by 2030 which we expect to contribute to 3% of our electricity generation needs, and also, that we are going to have an emissions target for 2030 and 2050.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And in relation to these, if I may ask, if the Ministry would consider setting a target mix for the amount of electricity that is going to be generated from renewable energy sources as a target that we can strive for together as a nation?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If we look at the IEA estimates, at present, globally, about 30% of the electricity generation is really from renewable sources.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I recognise that we have geographical constraints but is that perhaps a goal that we can strive towards, especially when we are already considering new green energy sources such as hydrogen, which I recognise that the EMA is already studying.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The second is in relation to the calculation of electrical tariffs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Right now, given that 95% of the energy mix is derived from natural gas, I think the fuel cost component is pretty much based on average natural gas prices, especially if future transmission from regional grids are involved.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: How then would the fuel costs as well as network costs component be calculated, and how would that be passed on to consumers at the end of the day?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To the first point, in terms of working on the target, indeed, we are and we have been looking at the different technologies that are available at this particular point in time.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Also, through working with the research institutions, the universities and so on, to see how we can also take on some of these initiatives with regard to carbon capture utilisation to see how we can set that target.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In due time we would be able to share that, once a more definitive landing on some of these technologies are available.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To reach that target by 2030 should not be a major problem.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In fact, we hope that we can do even better than that.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: With regard to the electricity tariffs, it is, at this particular point in time, still a fairly commercial venture.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As I have alluded to earlier on, the pricing will be competitive.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There will be an open transparent bidding process and this electricity will then be sold into the Singapore Wholesale Electricity Market.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, I hope that that reassures the hon Member of Parliament.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Before I begin, let me declare that I am a senior executive for a gas and engineering company that deals with energy sources.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I want to thank Minister for his response on the diversification to ensure our energy needs over the years.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: But with respect to the fourth switch, I have this question for Minister.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: When it comes to dealing with low carbon energy sources or alternatives, the very key aspects are around policies and the other one around subsidies and fundings.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Our current carbon tax programme is actually very low compared to many countries in the world and we have a very low target that we want to achieve by 2030 and beyond.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: So, I want to know how this lever is going to impact the kind of low-carbon alternatives we will have in future.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: And for the other aspect around subsidies – will the Government look at more options apart from just funding the technology programmes, but directly subsidising some of the very attractive alternatives in order for us to achieve this target of decarbonisation, earlier than later.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For the carbon tax, even if we raise the carbon tax significantly, it is not going to move the needle that much in terms of the overall pricing.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Where we are now looking at is also, as I have said, the fourth switch.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It is not just about carbon capture, utilisation and storage; it is also looking at hydrogen utilisation and leveraging on this hydrogen technology.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To that end, EMA and the Ministry are actively pursuing significant projects to see how we can, not just extract the hydrogen, but also in terms of the transportation of that hydrogen.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If we are able to tap on it, it is going to be the cleanest fuel, the byproduct of which is water.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These are the few big initiatives that we are currently embarking on today.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Other than carbon capture, we are also exploring employing carbon credits and contemplating some form of a carbon trading platform so that we can leverage on the multiple initiatives that are available to help us reduce our carbon footprint.
